name: ITensors.jl (Julia) vs C++ ITensor v3.1.6 in ITensorBenchmarks.jl
baseline: C++ ITensor v3.1.6 (github.com/ITensor/ITensor), same tensor-network algorithms, Intel MKL BLAS/LAPACK on both sides
workload: Wall-clock time of DMRG (1D Heisenberg dense and with QN block sparsity, 2D QN and 2D conserve_ky), TRG and CTMRG runs at increasing maximum bond dimension, 1 BLAS thread and 1 block-sparse thread, ITensors.jl v0.1.37 against C++ ITensor v3.1.6; per-run seconds are one number per maxdim_N.txt file under data/julia/v0.1.37 and data/c++/v3.1.6.
claimed_speedup: Julia faster at large bond dimension: DMRG 2D conserve_ky maxdim 10000 6245.4 s vs C++ 8944.8 s (1.43x, derived from page data); maxdim 1000 622.8 s vs 1035.0 s (1.66x); DMRG 1D QN maxdim 1000 173.2 s vs 225.0 s (1.30x); DMRG 1D dense maxdim 1000 3323.7 s vs 3857.2 s (1.16x); DMRG 2D QN maxdim 5000 6430.1 s vs 6721.0 s (1.05x). Julia slower at small sizes: DMRG 2D QN maxdim 1000 405.8 s vs 334.8 s; DMRG 1D QN maxdim 200 18.0 s vs 16.9 s; TRG maxdim 10 1.11 s vs 0.16 s; CTMRG maxdim 50 2.33 s vs 0.92 s. Near parity: TRG maxdim 50 256.6 s vs 264.2 s; CTMRG maxdim 400 104.7 s vs 115.8 s.
compiler_and_flags: C++ side: deps/options.mk.sample builds with g++ -m64 -std=c++17 -fconcepts -fPIC, OPTIMIZATIONS=-O2 -DNDEBUG, MKL (-lmkl_intel_lp64 -lmkl_intel_thread -liomp5); the options.mk actually used is not committed. Julia flags and version for the data run not stated (data directory is named v0.1.37, the ITensors.jl release).
tradeoffs: Needs the Julia runtime and JIT warm-up (the small-size rows are slower than C++, plausibly from startup and compile overhead, not stated by the source). Julia version adds splitblocks (sparser MPO), absent from C++ ITensor; the plain runs above do not use it. C++ ITensor stays the smaller dependency for embedding in C++ programs.
caveats: Numbers read from the raw .txt files under data/ (for example https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ITensor/ITensorBenchmarks.jl/HEAD/data/c++/v3.1.6/bench_dmrg_2d_conserve_ky/blas_num_threads_1/blocksparse_num_threads_1/maxdim_10000.txt and the same path under data/julia/v0.1.37); the benchmark_url tree page lists the folders only. No CPU model for this data (the TeNPy comparison page in the same repo names 4 x Xeon Gold 6128 for its own runs only). Data dates from Feb 2021 (last benchmark repo commit 2021-12-06, stale); ITensors.jl and C++ ITensor have both changed since. C++ built with -O2 per the sample options, not -O3. Single runs, no variance reported. The ITensor software library paper (arXiv 2007.14822, SciPost Phys. Codebases 2022, snippet only, not opened) says Julia is very competitive with C++ and fastest for some block-sparse algorithms; the verifier may lift the tier if the paper's figures match these data. Win is mostly large bond dimension, the Julia code is not uniformly faster.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Julia package faster than C++ library tensor contraction OR sparse OR quadrature OR ODE benchmark comparison blog repository' surfaced the ITensor library paper snippet and github.com/ITensor/ITensorBenchmarks.jl

name: Clarabel.rs (Rust interior-point conic and QP solver) vs ECOS in qpbenchmark Maros-Meszaros
baseline: ECOS 2.0.14 (C interior-point conic solver, also homogeneous self-dual embedding based)
workload: Solve time (shifted geometric mean, shift 10, failed solves scored at the 1000 s limit) over the 62-problem dense subset of the Maros-Meszaros QP test set, four tolerance settings, solvers called from Python through qpsolvers 4.3.3.
claimed_speedup: Dense subset shifted geometric mean runtime, Clarabel 0.9.0 vs ECOS 2.0.14: default 20793.9 vs 126497.0 (6.1x lower, derived from page data), low accuracy 20.1 vs 112.3 (5.6x), mid accuracy 116.6 vs 652.7 (5.6x), high accuracy 26095.2 vs 171259.8 (6.6x); success rate at default settings 51.6% vs 12.9%. On the full 138-problem set Clarabel (163.8) is slower than OSQP (12.7), SCS (15.1) and HiGHS (30.7); ECOS is not in that table.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated; solvers are PyPI builds (clarabel 0.9.0, ecos 2.0.14) run from Python 3.12.4 through qpsolvers 4.3.3.
hardware: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-6500U CPU @ 2.50GHz (4 logical CPUs), run 2024-09-07 by the qpbenchmark author
stars_or_usage: 617 stars; default QP/conic solver in CVXPY per the paper snippet
tradeoffs: Rust crate with Python (pip install clarabel) and a separate Julia port (oxfordcontrol/Clarabel.jl); handles quadratic objectives natively; interior-point solves are dense in iterations but high accuracy, whereas ADMM solvers (OSQP, SCS) are cheaper per problem at low accuracy.
caveats: The ECOS runtime figure is inflated by its 12.9% success rate because failed solves are charged the 1000 s time limit. The same independent suite shows Clarabel behind OSQP (C), SCS (C), HiGHS (C++) and PIQP (C++) on the full and sparse sets at default settings, so the library is not a general win over C solvers. Python wrapper overhead is included for every solver. The Mathematical Programming Computation paper (Goulart and Chen, arXiv 2405.12762; search snippet only, arxiv.org and the paper tables not opened) is the source of the broader 'faster than commercial and open-source solvers on QPs' claim, and a WebSearch snippet of an older qpsolvers report (3.5.0) gave Clarabel best runtime on a hard subset; the 2024-09 reports opened here do not repeat that.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Clarabel interior point solver Rust benchmark faster than ECOS OSQP SCS Maros Meszaros results'; github.com/topics/convex-optimization?l=rust
why_faster: README (Clarabel.rs and Clarabel.jl): unlike solvers based on the standard homogeneous self-dual embedding, it handles quadratic objectives without epigraphical reformulation, so it can be significantly faster than other HSDE-based solvers on problems with quadratic objectives.

name: FFTA.jl (pure Julia FFT) vs FFTW.jl on small static vectors
workload: One @btime of fft on a 64-element StaticArrays SVector of Float64, FFTA.fft vs FFTW.fft, as shown in the FFTA.jl README.
claimed_speedup: N=64 SVector: FFTA.fft 698.611 ns (8 allocations, 2.11 KiB) vs FFTW.fft 5.433 us (34 allocations, 4.70 KiB), about 7.8x (derived from page data); the README itself calls the example cherry-picked.
tradeoffs: Pure Julia and generic over element types (BigFloat, symbolic, StaticArrays), only 1D and 2D; the README itself says to use FFTW.jl for more performance.
caveats: Single README snippet, no CPU, Julia version or flags. FFTW.fft(x) on an SVector converts to an Array and builds a plan on every call (our reading of how FFTW.jl's fft works, not stated by the source), so the timing largely measures planning and allocation, not transform speed. The repo's benchmark/ suite (separate Julia environments for FFTA and FFTW, fft($x) with a fresh plan each call) has no committed results and the README steers users to FFTW.jl for speed. Not a general speedup claim; probably slower than FFTW with a reused plan.
found_via: Blogs / talks: README read while screening Julia numerics packages from github.com/topics/linear-algebra?l=julia and the JuliaMath organisation
why_faster: README: carrying Julia's type specialisation (generic code that works on small StaticArrays without heap workspace) into the FFT; no further mechanism given.
